title: The Law Committee
hook: Conservative rabbis rule on questions like driving to synagogue on Shabbat

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Masorti, and your line was tradition and change: halakha as binding, and halakha with a history. Did you learn one Conservative ruling? Today, the room where rulings like that get made. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-two.

Saturday morning. A family is dressed for synagogue. The building is across town, too far for the grandmother to walk, too far for the kids. The car is sitting in the driveway. For a family that keeps Shabbat, that car is a real question, because Shabbat is a day without kindling fire, and rabbis have long treated starting an engine as part of that. So what do they do? Stay home and miss praying with their community? Or drive, only there and only back? A question like that, in the Conservative movement, doesn't get settled at the kitchen table. It goes to a committee.
screen: `SATURDAY, A CAR IN THE DRIVEWAY.` → `TOO FAR TO WALK.` → `A QUESTION FOR THE COMMITTEE.`

segments.voice: The Law Committee. Its full name is the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, and it belongs to the Conservative movement's association of rabbis. Its job is old work in a new room. Long before any committee, when a Jew had a hard question of law, they wrote to a scholar, and the scholar wrote back. The answer is called a teshuvah, a response. The committee writes teshuvot too, with sources, arguments and a conclusion. Start with the text behind the driving question. The Torah says, "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." The verse is short. The hard part was weighing two goods. Shabbat rest is one. Praying together is another. The committee's answer, as it is usually told, was that a family living too far to walk could drive to synagogue on Shabbat, and home again, and nowhere else. The reasoning was not that Shabbat matters less. It was that losing the community's prayer would cost Shabbat more. Now the second thing to know about this committee. It can approve more than one answer to the same question. Then the rabbi of each congregation, called the mara d'atra, the master of the place, chooses which one that community follows. So some Conservative synagogues accepted the driving ruling, and some Conservative Jews still walk every Shabbat. Orthodox authorities hold that driving on Shabbat is forbidden, and they reach that answer from the same texts. Two movements, one Torah, different weighings. That is today's line: law that develops, one written answer at a time.
screen: `A TESHUVAH: A WRITTEN ANSWER.` · `NO FIRE ON SHABBAT.` · `TWO GOODS TO WEIGH.` · `MORE THAN ONE ANSWER CAN STAND.` · then, large: `YE SHALL KINDLE NO FIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: consider one ruling's reasons. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the family and the car. Hold the first good in one hand: a day of rest, with no fire, no engine, no errands. Hold the second in the other: the grandmother, the kids, the prayers said together. Don't decide. Just feel the weight of each, the way a committee would have to. Then ask yourself which is harder: judging an answer, or writing one. The bell holds the time.

The Law Committee. The Conservative movement's committee that answers questions of Jewish law in writing, can approve more than one answer, and leaves the choice to each congregation's rabbi. Today's word.
Your line: law that develops. Today, when you hear a rule you disagree with, try to name the two goods it is weighing before you argue with it. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: In the Conservative movement, rabbis bring questions of Jewish law to the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, which answers in written responsa; each congregation's rabbi decides which approved answer the community follows.
